newsitem.title: USA: Grains fall on good weather, coffee soars.
newsitem.headline: Grains fall on good weather, coffee soars.

text.p: Grain and soybean prices fell Tuesday as harvest weather in the Midwest improved, while coffee prices rose on tightness in near-term supplies.
In other markets, gasoline prices bucked a lower trend in energy markets after a refinery fire, and copper prices fell after miner Kennecott Copper and its Utah unions avoided a strike.
The Commodity Research Bureau of 17 futures prices ended down 1.43 points at 244.20.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices led the declines as the National Weather Service six-to-10 day outlook predicted ideal harvesting weather in the Midwest.
November soybeans closed 8-3/4 cents per bushel lower at $7.49-1/4 and December corn down 3/4 cent a bushel at $2.96.

Traders said selling by professional speculative funds who had been betting on cold weather hurting the late-maturing crops continued to pressure prices lower, along with selling by commercial firms tat were selling futures contracts to hedge the corn the newly harvested grain they were buying on cash markets.
"It's continued fund liquidation. The crop conditions improved and the six-to-10 day certainly wasn't friendly," said analyst Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.

On Monday afternoon, the U.S. Agriculture Department rated the U.S. soybean crop condition as 57 percent good or excellent, up two percentage points from a week earlier. The corn ratings increased by a similar margin.
Improved weather also aided emergence of winter wheat from the High Plains to the eastern Midwest.
December wheat closed 2-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $4.33-3/4 on the brighter outlook for next year's supplies.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, December coffee rose a strong 1.80 cents a pound to 104.75 cents after weekly warehouse inventory data showed stockpiles at their lowest level in more than a decade.
A drop of 10,000 bags in exchange-certified warehouses sent stocks to a 12-year low of 31,669 bags as of September 27, catching many traders by surprise.
But analysts said with newly harvested Brazilian and Colombia supplies due soon, the gains may be short-lived.
"Coffee prices are not going to go up much more because the coffee harvest is coming," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "Pretty soon, we will be knee-deep in coffee."
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil closed lower on worries about possible approval of a United Nations deal to allow Iraq oil sales to buy humanitarian supplies.
November crude ended 24 cents a barrel lower at $24.14.

Iraq's Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf said he saw a consensus among foreign ministers at a UN General Assembly meeting for a speedy implementation of the deal, which was approved in May but frozen by Iraqi troop attacks on Kurds last month.

Under the deal, trade sanctions imposed on Iraq over its 1990 invasion of Kuwait would be lifted by the United Nations, and Iraq would be allowed to export $2 billion of oil in exchange for humanitarian aid.

But oil product prices rose after a refinery fire at a Conoco Inc. refinery in Louisiana fed buying in gasoline amid trader talk the company shut its 51,000 barrel per day cat cracker at the Lake Charles plant.
November unleaded gasoline closed 0.56 cent a gallon higher at 62.82 cents and November heating oil ended up 0.01 cent a gallon at 70.76 cents.
Conoco later said that while three workers were injured in the Monday evening blaze, refinery operations were unaffected at the 180,000 bpd refinery.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division, prices ended lower after mining company Kennecott Copper and its Utah labour unions said they would continue talks despite expiration of a labour contract at midnight on Monday.
December copper ended 2.25 cents lower at 87.85 cents a pound.

The news spurred traders to largely ignore a strong drawdown in European stocks, usually a good sign of cash demand. Copper stockpiles at the London Metal Exchange warehouses fell 7,825 metric tons to 239,500 tons.
"The draw down on LME was quite constructive, but the market was hoping for higher numbers," said Bette Raptopoulos of Prudential Securities.
